Lebanon Grapples with Currency Collapse as Businesses Recoil

Lebanon is reeling from a dramatic collapse of its currency, with the Lebanese pound losing over 60% of its value against the US dollar in just the past two weeks, sparking widespread turmoil across the country’s economy. The ongoing crisis has led to surging prices for everyday goods, stalled imports, and mounting uncertainty among businesses and workers.

The exchange rate, which hovered around 90,000 Lebanese pounds to the dollar at the start of June, plunged to over 150,000 by Thursday, according to traders in Beirut. The central bank has struggled to intervene due to dwindling reserves, and many commercial banks have suspended foreign currency transactions altogether.

Major employers have already begun to feel the impact. Holcim Liban SAL, one of the country’s largest cement producers, announced this week that it has temporarily reduced output at its Chekka plant due to difficulties in importing raw materials and spare parts, as well as a sharp drop in local demand.

“Our industry relies on stable exchange rates for both equipment and supplies,” said a spokesperson for Holcim Liban SAL. “With costs changing daily and clients unable to pay, we are forced to scale back operations.”

Other companies are facing similar challenges. A manager at United Textiles, a large garment manufacturer based in Sidon, said, “We can’t pay our suppliers abroad, and our workers’ salaries lose value every week. We’re holding on, but it’s getting harder.”

The Lebanese Chamber of Commerce warned in a statement that “business closures and layoffs are inevitable if currency volatility continues unchecked.” The union representing construction workers echoed these concerns, reporting a surge in job losses in the past fortnight.

As the crisis deepens, economists caution that Lebanon’s fragile social safety nets are ill-prepared for the fallout. “If the government cannot stabilize the currency soon, we risk a protracted economic depression,” said Dr. Hani El-Masri, an economist at the Lebanese National University.
